summary: Describes a conflict between TCP and Differentiated Services over the use of the three leftmost bits of the IPv4 TOS octet. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 9293.

eli5.summary: Two sets of rules wanted to use the same part of a packet's label for different jobs. This explains the clash and how TCP should behave.

questions: why do tcp and diffserv conflict
what is the ipv4 precedence field
subtitle: How to resolve a conflict between TCP and DiffServ over packet priority bits.

tldr.problem: TCP and Differentiated Services (DiffServ) both claim the same three bits in the IPv4 TOS octet: TCP uses them for connection precedence, while DiffServ uses them for quality-of-service markings. Network nodes modifying these bits for QoS break TCP connections.
tldr.mechanism: TCP is modified to ignore the precedence field entirely, eliminating the conflict. TCP no longer requires precedence to match during connection setup or while connected, allowing DiffServ nodes to freely modify those bits.
tldr.outcome: TCP connections become resilient to precedence changes in transit. The RFC was superseded by RFC 9293, which consolidated this and related changes to TCP.

today: RFC 2873 was a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 9293, which consolidated TCP modifications and provided an updated, unified specification.

sections.title: The Precedence and Quality-of-Service Conflict
sections.content:
The IPv4 header contains an octet called the TOS (Type of Service) field. The three leftmost bits of this octet were traditionally used for precedence: a TCP application could request that its packets carry a particular priority level (from 0 for routine to 7 for network control). TCP required that all packets on a connection maintain the same precedence for the connection's lifetime.

Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a later standard for quality-of-service, repurposed those same three bits as the high-order part of the DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point). DiffServ-capable network nodes in the middle of the path modify these bits to indicate desired forwarding behavior, such as expedited forwarding or assured forwarding.

When DiffServ nodes modify the precedence bits for QoS purposes, TCP endpoints that still enforce precedence matching either fail to establish the connection or reset it mid-flow. This creates operational problems that make it impossible to deploy DiffServ in networks with precedence-aware TCP endpoints.
sections.eli5: A TCP connection says 'all my packets must say priority 3.' But a router in the middle says 'I will change this to priority 5 for quality reasons.' The TCP module sees the wrong priority and says 'this is broken, I am closing the connection.'

sections.title: The Pieces of the TOS Octet
sections.content:
The IPv4 TOS octet is divided into four parts. The leftmost three bits are the precedence field, which represent priority levels 0 through 7. Bits 3–6 are the TOS field, encoding desired service characteristics like low delay, high throughput, or high reliability. Bit 7 is MBZ (Must Be Zero), historically unused.

DiffServ redefines the octet as the DS Field. The leftmost six bits are the DSCP, which encodes the forwarding treatment (per-hop behavior) a packet should receive. The rightmost two bits are currently unused.

Because DSCP uses six bits and precedence uses three, the top three bits of DSCP directly overlap with the precedence bits. Any DSCP value will change the apparent precedence to TCP.
sections.eli5: Think of the packet label as having 8 positions. TCP reads the first 3 for 'priority.' DiffServ uses 6 positions for 'type of handling,' and those 6 happen to include the same first 3 spots.

sections.title: Four Problems from the Conflict
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four specific problems. Problem 1: during TCP connection setup (the three-way handshake), if the SYN or SYN-ACK packet's precedence bits are modified by the network, the receiving TCP endpoint may refuse to acknowledge the connection because the precedence does not match what was sent. Problem 2: after a connection is established, if any data packet's precedence is altered in transit, the receiving TCP endpoint must reset the connection.

Problem 3: two TCP endpoints might establish a connection with different precedence values because the network modified the precedence fields, causing both endpoints to incorrectly think they agreed. Problem 4: if one endpoint changes its own precedence during transmission and DiffServ nodes modify it back to the expected value, the connection will not reset as RFC 793 would require.

Each problem causes either unwanted connection failures or unwanted permissiveness, depending on circumstances. All four stem from TCP insisting that precedence must remain stable.
sections.eli5: Precedence changes break connections (problems 1 and 2), or they create false agreements or false disagreements (problems 3 and 4).

sections.title: The Solution: Ignore Precedence
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a simple fix: TCP must ignore the precedence field entirely. During connection setup, TCP ignores precedence in both directions; two endpoints can establish a connection even if the SYN and SYN-ACK packets carry different precedence values. After connection is established, each endpoint sends data with whatever precedence it chooses, and the receiving endpoint ignores the precedence of all incoming packets.

This change resolves problems 1 and 2 by making connection setup and data transfer immune to precedence modifications. Problems 3 and 4 become non-issues: there is no longer any requirement for precedence to match, so false agreements and false disagreements do not matter.

The trade-off is that TCP applications can no longer rely on precedence to influence network treatment. However, they can still use DSCP directly (outside of TCP) to request quality-of-service treatment from DiffServ nodes.
sections.eli5: TCP stops caring about the priority bits altogether, leaving them for DiffServ to control. No more conflicts.
